nameStory: American brooklime gets its name from its favorite hangout spot — brooks, streams, and other watery places where it thrives. The "lime" part comes from an old English word meaning "sticky" or "slimy," referring to the plant's smooth, somewhat succulent feel when you touch it. It's also called American speedwell, belonging to a group of plants once thought to speed travelers on their way with good luck.
description: American brooklime is a low-growing perennial wildflower that loves to get its feet wet in streams and soggy areas. This smooth, hairless plant sprawls along the ground or floats partially in water, growing anywhere from 4 inches to over 3 feet long. Its small, soft violet-blue flowers bloom in delicate clusters above pairs of narrow, toothed leaves. The whole plant has a fresh, clean appearance that matches its preference for clear, flowing water.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny soft violet or pale blue flowers with four petals, clustered in loose spikes that emerge from where leaves meet the stem. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch across with delicate white lines radiating from the center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Feel smooth and slightly thick to the touch, with small teeth along the edges that you can feel with your fingertip.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling or creeping plant that often trails in shallow water or spreads across wet mud. Stems feel smooth and round when rolled between your fingers, never square.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Completely hairless, smooth stems that are distinctly round in cross-section. They often root at joints where they touch the ground or water, creating new plants.

habitat: Look for American brooklime along the edges of clear streams, brooks, and springs throughout New England's forests and meadows. It thrives in shallow, slow-moving water or on muddy banks that stay consistently moist. You'll often find it growing alongside watercress, wild mint, and sedges in these cool, shaded waterways.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green shoots along stream edges. Early flowers may begin appearing in late spring in warmer, sunny spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with clusters of small violet flowers most visible from June through August. The plant is lush and green, often forming mats in suitable habitat.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, though less profusely. Leaves remain green and fresh-looking well into autumn thanks to the constant moisture.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the roots in most of New England, though some stems may persist under ice or in spring-fed areas that don't freeze completely.

funFact: American brooklime is one of nature's water quality indicators — it only grows in clean, unpolluted water, so finding a healthy patch tells you the stream is in good ecological shape!
confusionNotes: Often confused with members of the mint family like skullcaps, but here's the key difference: roll the stem between your fingers. Mints have distinctly square stems that feel angular, while brooklime has perfectly round, smooth stems. Also, mint family flowers are typically more tubular, while brooklime's are flat and open.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "brooklime," this plant is completely unrelated to the citrus lime fruit. The name comes from Old English and refers to the plant's texture, not its taste or smell.
compareHints: Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group. While most other speedwells prefer dry fields, lawns, or woodlands, brooklime is almost always found with its roots in water or saturated soil. Its leaves are also notably longer and narrower than most of its relatives, and it's one of the few speedwells that forms spreading mats rather than staying in neat clumps.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
